en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Second Chapter
The Discourse on Embers:
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, embers?
Yes, they are.
Is it not the case that there is pleasant feeling: bodily pleasure, mental pleasure, celestial pleasure, human pleasure,
the pleasure of gain, the pleasure of honor, the pleasure of transport, the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of sovereignty, the pleasure of lordship,
the pleasure of a householder, the pleasure of a recluse, tainted pleasure, untainted pleasure, the pleasure of acquisitions, and the pleasure free from acquisitions?
Is there carnal pleasure, spiritual pleasure, pleasure accompanied by rapture, pleasure devoid of rapture, the pleasure of jhāna,
the pleasure of liberation, sensual pleasure, the pleasure of renunciation, the pleasure of seclusion, the pleasure of tranquility, and the pleasure of full enlightenment? Yes.
If there is pleasant feeling … [and so on] … up to the bliss of full enlightenment, then indeed, it should not be said:
"All conditioned phenomena, without exception, are a pit of embers."
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, burning embers? Yes.
Are all conditioned phenomena painful feeling—bodily pain, mental pain, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
It should not be said so.
Should it not be said that "all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā), without exception, are burning embers"?
“Yes, [it is so].
“But was it not said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, everything is ablaze’?”
And what, monks, is all that is aflame?
The eye, monks, is aflame; forms are aflame; eye-consciousness is aflame; eye-contact is aflame;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is aflame.
“By what is it ablaze?
“It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—this I say.
The ear is ablaze, sounds are ablaze... [and so on].”
The nose is ablaze, odors are ablaze ...
the tongue is ablaze, tastes are ablaze ...
the body is ablaze, tangibles are ablaze ... [and so forth].
The mind is aflame; mental phenomena are aflame; mind-consciousness is aflame; mind-contact is aflame.
Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is aflame.
By what is it aflame?
“I say it is set ablaze by the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is set ablaze by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
In that case, it should be said:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā), without exception, are burning embers.
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, burning embers?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘Bhikkhus, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure’?”
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … [and so on] …
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”
Is it indeed a sutta? Yes.
Therefore, it should not be said—
“Without exception, all conditioned phenomena are burning.
Is it not the case that one should say,
“Without exception, all conditioned phenomena are burning”?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘It is a gain for you, bhikkhus; it is a great acquisition for you, bhikkhus, that you have obtained the opportunity to dwell in the holy life’?”
“Monks, I have seen the hells called ‘the six bases of contact.

There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only what is unattractive, not what is attractive; only what is disagreeable, not what is agreeable; only what is unpleasant, not what is pleasant.
Whatever sound one hears with the ear... [and so on for the other sense objects].”
One smells an odor with the nose...
one tastes a flavor with the tongue...
one touches a tangible object with the body...

"One cognizes a mental object with the mind; one cognizes only what is undesirable, not what is desirable; one cognizes only what is unlovely, not what is lovely; one cognizes only what is disagreeable, not what is agreeable.
Is this indeed a sutta? Yes.
In that case, it should be said:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā), without exception, are burning (kukkuḷā).
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, burning?
“Yes, [it is so].
“Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
‘It is a gain for you, monks, it is a great fortune for you, monks, that you have obtained the opportunity to dwell in the holy life’?”
“Monks, I have seen what are called the heavens consisting of the six bases of contact.

There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only a desirable form, not an undesirable form; one sees only a pleasing form, not a displeasing form; one sees only a lovely form, not an unlovely form.
Whatever sound one hears with the ear... [and so on for the other sense objects].”
One smells an odor with the nose;
one tastes a flavor with the tongue;
one touches a tangible object with the body.

“One cognizes a mental object with the mind; one cognizes only what is desirable, not what is undesirable; one cognizes only what is pleasant, not what is unpleasant; one cognizes only what is agreeable, not what is disagreeable.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā), without exception, are burning (kukkuḷā).
It should not be said.
“Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, a pit of embers?”—Yes.
But has it not been said by the Blessed One: “Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering”?
“Are all conditioned phenomena impermanent?”—Yes.
If so, since it was said by the Blessed One: “Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering.”
“‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent’—therefore, indeed, it should be said:
‘All conditioned phenomena, without exception, are a pit of embers.
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, a pit of embers?”
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is giving a fruit that is undesirable, a fruit that is unlovely, a fruit that is disagreeable, a fruit that is distressing, having suffering as its source, and having suffering as its result?
You should not speak thus.
Virtue … [and so on] … the Uposatha … [and so on] … development … [and so on].
Is the holy life (brahmacariya) of undesirable fruit, of unpleasant fruit, of disagreeable fruit, of fruit that causes one to weep, having suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?
One should certainly not say so.
Is it not the case that giving (dāna) has desirable fruit, pleasant fruit, agreeable fruit, fruit that does not cause one to weep, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result?
“Yes.
“If giving has desirable fruit, pleasant fruit, agreeable fruit, gratifying fruit, and results in happiness and a happy ripening, then indeed it should not be said:
‘All conditioned phenomena, without exception, are a pit of embers.’”
Is it not the case that virtue … the Uposatha … and development [are likewise]?
Is the holy life (brahmacariya) one that has desirable fruit, lovely fruit, agreeable fruit, and inexhaustible fruit, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result?
Yes.

If the holy life has desirable fruit, lovely fruit, agreeable fruit, and inexhaustible fruit, having happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result, then indeed, it should not be said: [that it is otherwise].
“All conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) are, without exception, a pit of embers.
Are all conditioned phenomena, without exception, a pit of embers? Yes.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
"Blissful is seclusion for one who is contented,
who has heard the Dhamma, and who sees"?
Harmlessness is happiness in the world,
restraint toward living beings;
dispassion for the world is happiness.
The transcending of sensual desires,
and the subduing of the conceit "I am"—
this indeed is the supreme happiness.
Having attained happiness through happiness,
that is indeed ultimate happiness;
the three types of higher knowledge have been realized.
“This indeed is the supreme happiness.
Is this truly a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it should not be said that "all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā), without exception, are burning embers" (kukkuḷa).
The Discussion on Burning Embers is finished.
